title: Autocomplete Was Like a Helpful Passenger. Agents Took the Wheel.

panels.text: In Issue 7, we watched language models learn to write code. You could type a question into a chat window, and an LLM would hand you a function, a class, an entire module. Extraordinary.

But there was a catch. You still had to copy the code, run it yourself, read the errors, go back to the chat, and ask for a fix. It was like having a brilliant advisor locked in a soundproof room — they could slip you a plan under the door, but you had to do all the running.

panels.prompt: Close-up of a dark terminal screen with a blinking cursor, no human hands visible, soft out-of-focus green text in the background, the cursor blinking steadily at a command prompt, sense of quiet automation and precision, clean and modern atmosphere. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, dark background with violet (#9F7AEA) accent highlights

A terminal screen showing the triumphant final output: bright green text reading 'Task complete. All 14 tests passing.' with a glowing green checkmark, confetti-like particles of light around the text, sense of accomplishment and automation, dark terminal background. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, violet and green accent lighting

panels.text: Between 2021 and 2025, that wall came down. AI went from suggesting code to writing, running, testing, debugging, and fixing code — all on its own. The advisor left the room and sat down at the keyboard.

panels.caption: The Four Leaps from autocomplete to autonomous agents

panels.text: For 80 years, we made computers easier for humans to use. Now we are making computers that use themselves. The shift from “AI writes code” to “AI does the work” is not just a feature upgrade — it is a fundamental change in what a computer can do.
The first leap happened in June 2021, when a VS Code extension made millions of developers feel like they had a mind reader sitting inside their editor.
